title: DC, Servo or Stepper?
description: Three motors, three very different jobs. Here's the decision, boiled down to three questions.

content.value: You've now met all three motor types this course uses. Picking the right one for a job isn't guesswork — it comes down to answering three questions about what the job actually needs.

1. Does it need to spin continuously, with no fixed end position?
     yes -> DC motor

2. Does it need to hold one precise angle, within a limited range?
     yes -> Servo

3. Does it need precise, repeatable, possibly multi-turn positioning?
     yes -> Stepper

Notice these aren't really competing on "which is best" — a DC motor spinning ARIA's wheels forever has nothing in common with the job of holding a sensor head at a fixed 30° tilt, which has nothing in common with reliably counting exact steps for a robot arm joint. Different jobs, different tools.

content.title: 🔧 Which motor for this job?
content.prompt: Read the job, then decide: DC, servo, or stepper?

tasks.label: Spinning ARIA's drive wheel, continuously, no fixed endpoint
tasks.explain: Continuous rotation with no target angle is exactly a DC motor's job.

tasks.label: Holding a camera at a fixed 45° tilt and staying there
tasks.explain: A single precise angle that has to be actively held is a servo's specialty.

tasks.label: A robot arm joint that needs to reliably return to an exact position, turn after turn
tasks.explain: Repeatable, countable, possibly multi-turn precision without needing a feedback sensor is what steppers are built for.

tasks.label: A small conveyor belt motor that just needs to keep turning at a set speed
tasks.explain: Continuous rotation again, no need to know or hold a specific angle.

tasks.label: Sweeping ARIA's ultrasonic sensor head between 0° and 90° to scan a room
tasks.explain: A bounded, precise range of angles that needs to be commanded and held — classic servo territory.

tasks.label: Moving a 3D printer's axis a precise, repeatable distance, over and over
tasks.explain: Exact, repeatable, countable positioning without a feedback sensor — the same reason steppers show up in 3D printers everywhere.

content.value: Real designs often mix all three on one robot — exactly like ARIA does: DC motors for the wheels, servos aiming sensors, and (in later modules) steppers where precise multi-turn joints are needed.
Key takeaway: choose DC for continuous rotation with no fixed endpoint, servo for a precise held angle within a limited range, and stepper for precise, repeatable, possibly multi-turn positioning.

quiz.question: A job needs continuous rotation with no target angle at all. Which motor fits?
quiz.explain: No fixed endpoint to hold or count towards — that's exactly what a plain DC motor is for.

quiz.question: A job needs to hold one precise, bounded angle and actively resist being pushed off it. Which motor fits?
quiz.explain: Actively holding and correcting a specific angle is the servo's feedback loop doing exactly its job.

quiz.question: Why might a stepper be chosen over a servo for a job needing many full rotations of precise, repeatable positioning?
options: A servo's range is limited by its potentiometer; a stepper can keep counting steps indefinitely
quiz.explain: Servos are typically bounded to a limited range like 0–180°. Steppers have no such limit — they just keep counting steps.
